title: Suraqa's horse
hookLine: Suraqa, chasing for the reward, sinks in the sand and turns back (Bukhari)

cards: A price on two heads. In Sahih al-Bukhari, Suraqa ibn Malik tells this story himself.
Messengers from Quraysh came to his tribe, offering a reward to anyone who killed or captured the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, or Abu Bakr.
Suraqa was sitting with his people when a man walked up: I just saw figures moving along the coast. I think it's them. Suraqa knew it was.
And he said out loud: no, that's just some travelers we know. He wanted the reward for himself. Today: Suraqa's horse.

teach.b: He waits a little, goes home, and quietly sends his horse out behind a hill. He takes his spear and rides. As he nears them, his horse stumbles and throws him.
In his own telling, he draws lots with divining arrows, the custom of the time, and the answer comes out against him: don't harm them.

teach.h: CLOSE ENOUGH TO HEAR HIM RECITE.
teach.b: He rides anyway, close enough, he says, to hear the Prophet reciting. He notices the Prophet doesn't look back, while Abu Bakr keeps turning around to look. Then the ground gives way.

teach.h: THE HORSE SINKS TO THE KNEES.
teach.b: His horse's forelegs sink into the earth up to the knees, and he's thrown. He urges the horse up; it can barely pull its legs out, and when it stands, dust rises from the tracks of its legs like smoke.
He draws lots again, and again the answer is the one he doesn't want. At last Suraqa does what a hunter doesn't do.
He calls out to the men he's chasing and asks for safety. They stop. He tells them everything: the reward, what people are planning.
He offers them food and supplies. They take nothing.

They ask only, in effect: keep our matter hidden. He asks for a written promise of safety, and Amir ibn Fuhayra, Abu Bakr's freed man, writes it for him on a piece of leather. The fugitives never run faster.

The chaser is the one who's stopped, by the ground and by his own lots, until he gives up the chase himself. The man who set out to sell them ends up guarding their secret, holding their promise in his hand.

how: Muslims retell Suraqa ibn Malik's chase from his own account in Sahih al-Bukhari as part of the hijrah story.

o: a horse Suraqa gave them for the road
the fast mount the travelers escaped on
the horse that sank as Suraqa gave chase

p: offered a reward for the two

s: the travelers outran Suraqa on fast camels
they never outran him; his horse sank and he gave up the chase.
Suraqa tells the story himself in Bukhari
it is his own account, from the reward to the leather.
the travelers took Suraqa's food and supplies
they took nothing and asked only that he keep their matter hidden.

games.q: you're Suraqa. your horse has sunk into the ground and thrown you, again. the men you're chasing are just ahead. what do you do?
o: climb back on and ride harder.
call out to them and ask for safety.
go home and send others after them.
games.why: he called out for safety, told them about the reward, and asked for a written promise, which they gave him on leather.

practice: Think of something you're chasing right now, a win, an argument, someone's approval, and notice how it feels to keep riding after it.

Then picture your horse's legs slowing in soft sand, and instead of fighting it, let it stop, and ask what might happen if you called out instead of charging. If you pray, you can ask Allah to show you which chases to let go.

wordCard.voice: Suraqa's horse. In Bukhari, its legs sink into the ground as Suraqa chases the Prophet for the reward, until he gives up the chase and asks for safety. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the name Suraqa, of Suraqa ibn Malik ibn Ju'shum, who tells the story.

carryVoice: Your line: the sand held him back. Nobody outran anybody that day. That's day seven hundred sixty-eight.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3906 (Suraqa's account: the reward, the figures on the coast, the divining arrows, the horse sinking, the request for safety, the writing on leather)
